name: Tobin's q
statement: When the market values a firm's capital above what it costs to replace, it pays to build more; below that, it does not.
meaning: Tobin's q is the ratio of the market value of a firm's, or an economy's, physical capital to the cost of replacing that capital. It links financial markets to real investment: when q is greater than one, the market values installed capital above its replacement cost, so building new capital creates value and firms have an incentive to invest; when q is less than one, existing assets are worth less than it would cost to rebuild them, so it is cheaper to buy than to build and investment falls. In principle q gravitates toward one, where the marginal value of capital just equals its replacement cost. It is a foundational bridge between asset prices and capital spending.
mechanism: The ratio turns a firm's market valuation into a signal about whether to add capital. If a company can raise equity that the market prices above the cost of the plant and equipment that money would buy, issuing it and investing adds value, pushing q above one and drawing investment in until the gap closes; if the market prices its capital below replacement cost, q falls below one and investment dries up. Strictly the theory concerns marginal q, the value of one more unit of capital over its cost, but what can be measured is average q, the whole firm's value over its total replacement cost. Fumio Hayashi showed in 1982 that under constant returns and competitive markets the two coincide.

examples.text: A firm whose market value sits well above the replacement cost of its assets has q above one and a clear incentive to invest in new capacity.
When q is below one, acquiring an existing company or its assets is cheaper than constructing new capital, so mergers can look more attractive than greenfield investment.
Smithers and Wright's 2000 book 'Valuing Wall Street' used aggregate q to argue that late-1990s US equities were far above the replacement cost of their underlying capital, and so overvalued.

variants.name: Marginal versus average q
variants.text: The theory concerns marginal q, but only average q is observable; Hayashi's 1982 conditions, constant returns and competitive markets, are when the two are equal.

variants.name: Whole-market q
variants.text: The economy-wide version, comparing the total market value of corporate equity to the replacement cost of corporate capital, used to judge whether the stock market is over or undervalued.

whyItMatters: Tobin's q gave economics a clean, market-based theory of investment, tying a firm's decision to build capital directly to how financial markets value that capital, and it remains a standard tool in corporate finance and macroeconomics. As an aggregate measure it offers a long-run yardstick for whether equities are cheap or dear relative to the replacement cost of real assets, informing debates about bubbles and mean reversion. It was part of the body of work on financial markets for which James Tobin won the 1981 Nobel prize in economics, and it endures as a core link between Wall Street and the real economy.

working.text: read q above one as a signal to invest and below one as a signal to hold back or buy existing assets instead of building.
remember that investment is driven by marginal q, while the measurable figure is average q, and the two coincide only under specific conditions.

working.lead: Use it as a long-run gauge
working.text: treat aggregate q as a yardstick for whether the market is dear or cheap against real assets, not a short-term timing signal.

limits: Replacement cost is hard to measure, especially at the level of a whole economy, which makes q noisy in practice. Average q is a biased proxy for the marginal q that actually drives investment whenever Hayashi's conditions fail, under imperfect competition, market power, or non-constant returns. Intangible assets such as research, brands, and software are poorly captured in replacement-cost measures, biasing q upward, and the ratio relies on market prices reflecting fundamentals, so mispricing distorts its signal. Empirically q can stay far from one for long stretches, undermining the tidy story that it reverts quickly, so it is better as a long-run guide than a precise short-run rule.
misreadings: Average q should not be treated as marginal q without Hayashi's conditions of constant returns and competitive markets; conflating them is the common technical error. Q need not revert to exactly one quickly, since adjustment costs and frictions keep it away. It is related to, but not the same as, the price-to-book ratio, because book value is not replacement cost. A firm-level q above one is not automatically overvaluation, since it can reflect genuine growth prospects, intangibles, or monopoly rents. And Tobin's 1981 Nobel was for his broad analysis of financial markets, not specifically for q.
origin: Developed by James Tobin with William Brainard, in Brainard and Tobin's 1968 paper and Tobin's 1969 'A General Equilibrium Approach to Monetary Theory', with the marginal-average relationship clarified by Fumio Hayashi in 1982.

sources.text: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1981 (James Tobin), NobelPrize.org. — the award and the description of Tobin's q.
Hayashi, 'Tobin's Marginal q and Average q: A Neoclassical Interpretation,' Econometrica 50(1):213-224 (1982). — the conditions under which average q equals marginal q.
